target.title: Development of a Silent Speech Interface Driven by Ultrasound and Optical Images of the Tongue and Lips

read.pdf: Figures 1-10 and Tables 1-2 read from the accepted-manuscript PDF

entries.text: The proposed SSI maps ultrasound tongue and optical lip observations through phone recognition and corpus-based synthesis to a speech waveform.
entries.condition: The reported experiments use uttered speech; the system input at use time is visual data.
entries.quote: The system then combines a phone recognition stage with corpus-based synthesis.

entries.text: The proposed combination uses an HMM phone recognizer, visual-space diphone selection with an acoustic concatenation cost, and HNM waveform generation.
entries.condition: Audio-visual dictionary is built off-line from paired training data; synthesis is driven by the predicted phonetic targets.

entries.text: The audiovisual database contains one hour of continuous uttered speech per speaker from two native American English speakers, one male and one female.
entries.condition: Speaker A is female and speaker B is male; recorded tongue ultrasound, optical lip video, and acoustic speech together; speakers read displayed text neutrally; experiments use uttered, not silent, speech.

entries.text: CMU-Arctic contains 1,132 sentences in sets S1 and S2, with 593 and 539 items and reported diphone coverage of 78% and 75.4%.
entries.condition: CMU-Arctic text corpus, American English; S1 and S2 are phonetically balanced sets.

entries.text: The paper uses a 41-element American English phone set: 39 phonemes, schwa, and pause.
entries.condition: Phonetic labels and visual phone models for the American English corpus.

entries.text: Each speaker was recorded in one long session with no inter-session recalibration; the subjects remained fixed in HATS.
entries.condition: No recalibration between sessions was available or used.
entries.quote: Because no inter-session recalibration mechanism was employed, data was recorded in a single long session during which subjects remained fixed in the HATS system.

entries.text: Both speakers completed all S1, while S2 acquisition stopped at 80% because of fatigue, leaving 1,020 rather than 1,132 sentences before later cleaning.
entries.condition: Per speaker, before dropping the first 240 recordings from both databases and subsequent data cleaning.

entries.text: After cleaning, each speaker database contained roughly 45 minutes, 780 sentences, and 80,000 bitmap frames; audio sampling was 16 kHz.
entries.unit: per-speaker speech duration; sentences; frames; Hz audio sample rate
entries.condition: Cleaned databases A and B; the source corpus was continuous uttered speech.

entries.text: Speaker B's head/transducer shift after 240 sentences was not corrected; the first 240 sentences were dropped from both speakers, but later B alignment instability remained.
entries.condition: Shift was noticed during recording; remaining speaker B ultrasound frames were left as acquired.
entries.quote: This “accidental” displacement, which was noticed and reported by speaker B during the acquisition, occurred after the recording of 240 sentences.

entries.text: Tongue images came from an Aloka SSD-1000 with a 2.5-6 MHz convex probe, 120-degree scan angle, and a 7 cm single focal depth; image averaging and speckle reduction were disabled at acquisition.
entries.unit: ultrasound frequency; scan angle; focal depth
entries.condition: Midsagittal tongue slice; HATS fixed the probe beneath the chin; two cameras captured profile and lateral lip views, but only the frontal lip view was used for features.

entries.text: The analog NTSC system normalized the three video streams to 29.97 Hz.
entries.condition: Two optical cameras plus ultrasound and microphone audio combined in an analog video mixer.

entries.text: Image ROIs were resized to 64x64 and converted to grayscale; reduced ultrasound images were often processed with Yu and Acton's anisotropic diffusion filter.
entries.condition: Ultrasound ROI covers the vocal tract between mandible/hyoid shadows and short tendon/hyoid/palate; lip ROI is a bounding box, and the frontal lip view alone is used.

entries.text: PCA EigenTongue/EigenLips coding used typical 30-component tongue and 30-component lip projections, chosen empirically from image reconstruction quality.
entries.condition: A phonetically balanced subset of typical frames is used to construct the PCA space; the paper does not say whether it is restricted to each training fold.
entries.quote: Typical values of the pair (n, m) used on both database are (30, 30).

entries.text: Visual coefficients were linearly interpolated from 30 to 100 Hz (10 ms effective frame size); tongue and lip features plus first and second derivatives form typically 180-dimensional vectors.
entries.condition: Feature-fusion concatenation of tongue and frontal-lip PCA coefficients and their first and second derivatives.

entries.text: The authors report that LDA and DCT dimensionality-reduction alternatives did not improve recognition over the PCA image coding used in the study.
entries.condition: Compared on the authors' recognition results; no separate quantitative values are given.

entries.text: Visual phone sequences are modeled with continuous context-independent left-to-right HMMs having five states, including non-emitting initial and terminal states.
entries.unit: states per HMM, including two non-emitting states
entries.condition: Context-independent phone models; context-dependent models were not trained because the datasets were under one hour.
entries.quote: It was assumed that context-dependent models could not have been efficiently trained, even with parameter tying, because of the small size of our training datasets (less than one hour).

entries.text: The visual phone set has 41 models; phone transcriptions are generated from text using the CMU pronunciation dictionary, which covers over 125,000 words.
entries.condition: American English TIMIT phone transcription convention.
entries.quote: Phonetic transcription is derived from the text by using the CMU pronunciation dictionary, which transcribes over 125 000 words into phone sequences.

entries.text: HMMs were initialized by uniform flat-start segmentation, refined by incremental embedded training, and increased dyadically to at most 32 Gaussians per state using HTK.
entries.condition: Visual phone models; model complexity and transition penalty were selected using two jackknife validation experiments.

entries.text: At test time, the visual phone recognizer uses Token Passing through an HMM network.
entries.condition: Visual tongue/lip feature sequence; output is a phonetic target sequence.

entries.text: Three decoder grammars were tested: free phones; a word dictionary of 2,569 CMU-Arctic words; and a hybrid dictionary of 12,125 observed diphones/triphones plus corpus words.
entries.condition: Free-phonetic grammar permits every phone combination; word grammar permits all combinations of corpus words; hybrid uses observed corpus subword units plus corpus words.
entries.quote: In this scenario, the word dictionary contains 2569 items and the grammar allows all possible word combinations.

entries.text: The authors characterize hybrid decoding as a relatively weak linguistic constraint that keeps vocabulary open and appears suitable for generic applications.
entries.condition: The hybrid dictionary includes all CMU-Arctic diphones/triphones and words in the CMU-Arctic sentences; this is not an unrestricted external-vocabulary test.
entries.quote: Between these two extremes, the third scenario, with its relatively low level of linguistic constraint, appears most acceptable for a generic application.

entries.text: The 780 sentences per speaker were split into 26 lists of 30; each list served once as test while the other lists formed training data in a jackknife procedure.
entries.condition: Folds are within each speaker database, not speaker-held-out; the two speakers were evaluated separately.
entries.quote: For performance evaluation, the 780 sentences of databases A and B are divided into 26 lists of 30 sentences.

entries.text: Two of the 26 jackknife experiments were kept for validation to estimate Gaussian counts and inter-HMM transition penalties; parameters were chosen to maximize phoneme accuracy.
entries.condition: The paper does not identify the two fold indices or state exactly how Table 1 aggregates the remaining folds.
entries.quote: The jackknife procedure produces 26 (ideally independent) experiments, of which two are kept for validation.

entries.text: The phoneme accuracy is reported with a Wilson-formula 95% confidence half-interval; within-group confusions for listed phonetic equivalence classes are not counted as errors.
entries.condition: Phone accuracy uses test-reference phone count N and insertion, deletion, and substitution errors; equivalence classes include [er]/[r], [ih]/[iy], [uh]/[uw], [ao]/[ow], [aa]/[ah], and [sh]/[zh]; [zh] occurs 52 times in the database.

entries.text: Typical inter-model transition penalties were -100 for word-based and hybrid decoding and -20 for phone-based decoding.
entries.condition: Penalties were estimated on the validation experiments to limit insertions; the authors selected values to maximize phone accuracy.

entries.text: The acoustic reference decoder used 12 MFCCs plus energy and first/second derivatives, with 41 continuous left-to-right five-state HMMs and 32 Gaussians per state.
entries.condition: Acoustic features derived from the uttered-speech track; the paper calls this a best-possible comparison, not a silent-input baseline.

entries.text: Database A, phone-based decoding: acoustic P=80.8%, visual P=59.0%; reported 2Δ=1.0/1.2; D/S/I are 2087/2163/464 acoustic and 4614/4409/1039 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker A; phone-based (free phonetic) decoding; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation and equivalence-class scoring.

entries.text: Database A, hybrid decoding: acoustic P=85.8%, visual P=60.8%; reported 2Δ=0.9/1.2; D/S/I are 1780/1305/394 acoustic and 4711/4062/846 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker A; hybrid dictionary of CMU-Arctic words and observed subword units; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation.

entries.text: Database A, word-based decoding: acoustic P=89.6%, visual P=67.6%; reported 2Δ=0.8/1.2; D/S/I are 1305/923/318 acoustic and 3383/3567/984 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker A; decoder restricted to words in CMU-Arctic sentences; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation.

entries.text: Database B, phone-based decoding: acoustic P=77.3%, visual P=48.3%; reported 2Δ=1.0/1.3; D/S/I are 2397/2717/459 acoustic and 6362/5292/1027 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker B; phone-based (free phonetic) decoding; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation.

entries.text: Database B, hybrid decoding: acoustic P=83.1%, visual P=50.9%; reported 2Δ=0.9/1.3; D/S/I are 2145/1627/361 acoustic and 7040/4341/662 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker B; hybrid dictionary of CMU-Arctic words and observed subword units; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation.

entries.text: Database B, word-based decoding: acoustic P=86.2%, visual P=56.0%; reported 2Δ=0.9/1.2; D/S/I are 1550/1419/406 acoustic and 5388/4417/993 visual; N=24,496.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker B; decoder restricted to words in CMU-Arctic sentences; visual V versus acoustic A; jackknife evaluation.

entries.text: In all decoding scenarios for both modalities, word-based recognition is best, phone-based is worst, and hybrid is intermediate; the authors call hybrid appropriate for generic applications.
entries.condition: Table 1 comparisons across two speakers, audio/visual inputs, and the three dictionary constraint levels.

entries.text: A phone-based decoder with a simple training-set bigram language model improved accuracy by 0.7 percentage points over free phonetic decoding.
entries.unit: percentage points absolute phoneme accuracy improvement
entries.condition: Phone-based decoding; bigram model built from the training set; the authors say the hybrid scenario performs better.

entries.text: Low frame rate causes many visual phone deletions, especially for short gestures; [t] averages 65 ms and [ng] 126 ms in this database.
entries.condition: 30 fps source images are interpolated to 100 Hz; [t] is often represented by 1-2 source images, whereas [ng] by 3-4.

entries.text: Visual sensing omits voiced/unvoiced and nasality cues, and the tongue apex is often hidden by the mandible shadow, impairing dental-phone recognition.
entries.condition: Ultrasound tongue and lip video input only; discussed as recognition limitations.

entries.text: For speaker A in phone-based decoding, tongue-only accuracy was 55.9% versus 59.0% for tongue-plus-lips baseline and 39.0% for lips-only; D/S/I and N are also reported in Table 2.
entries.unit: P in % phoneme accuracy; 2Delta in percentage points; errors and N in phones
entries.condition: Speaker A; unconstrained phone-based decoding; feature modalities as named in Table 2.

entries.text: The authors say tongue-only recognition is 3.1 percentage points below fusion and suggest tongue images carry most information, while fusion may be suboptimal.
entries.condition: Speaker A; phone-based decoding; compared ultrasound-only with tongue-plus-lips Table 2 baseline.

entries.text: The authors describe visual phone recognition as promising relative to the acoustic decoder, with visual-to-acoustic accuracy ratio about 0.7 across decoding scenarios.
entries.condition: Ratio is for this database and all three decoding scenarios; acoustic reference uses the uttered-speech signal.

entries.text: The unit-selection method searches diphones by visual dynamic-time-warping target cost while penalizing acoustic MFCC discontinuity at concatenation points, using Viterbi path search.
entries.condition: Target and concatenation costs are weighted manually; audiovisual dictionary comes from forced alignment of the training database.
entries.quote: A unit selection algorithm first searches for the sequence of diphones that maximizes similarity to the input test data in visual space, while constraining unit concatenation in the acoustic domain.

entries.text: HNM waveform synthesis uses 12 harmonic components and a 16th-order autoregressive noise model.
entries.condition: Prosody-template pitch adaptation and smoothing at diphone boundaries.

entries.text: A training-corpus sentence with a comparable total phone count supplies the pitch template; pitch is median-smoothed, and no duration adaptation is implemented.
entries.condition: The template sentence is selected by total phone count only, not phone distribution; the target test sentence is excluded from training.

entries.text: Synthesis was evaluated with oracle phonetic transcription on 20 randomly chosen test sentences; the audiovisual unit dictionary was built from training data.
entries.condition: This isolates unit selection and HNM synthesis from phone-recognition errors; the paper does not identify the speaker/database for the selected sentences.
entries.quote: 20 test sentences are re-synthesized from their visual data alone, after first labeling it with the correct phonetic transcription.

entries.text: Seven native American English listeners transcribed synthesized and original sentences, hearing each sentence once; homophones were allowed and scoring was word-based.
entries.condition: Twenty sentences; this is a preliminary intelligibility test, not a full final-system evaluation.
entries.quote: Seven native speakers of American English were asked to transcribe the 20 synthesized sentences, as well as the corresponding original sentences.

entries.text: Original-sentence transcription accuracy averaged 97%, which the authors treat as the upper bound for this intelligibility test.
entries.condition: Original versions of the 20 sentences, transcribed by the same seven listeners, one listen per sentence; homophones allowed.

entries.text: With correct phone prediction, the authors conclude video-only data can yield a reasonably intelligible speech waveform; Figure 10 plots individual listener accuracies and confidence intervals.
entries.condition: Oracle phone sequence; 20 test sentences; seven native listeners; word-based transcription accuracy.

entries.text: Figure 10 shows listener-level synthesized-speech bars, but the paper does not tabulate exact per-listener values or a synthesized-speech aggregate accuracy in the text.
entries.condition: Seven listeners; 20 oracle-phone synthesized sentences; the figure uses a 0-100 axis and confidence intervals.
entries.quote: The results on the synthesized sentences are presented in Figure 10.

entries.text: Long-sentence intelligibility is often reduced by unrealistic rhythm, and consistently intelligible synthesis is not possible at the reported 66% visual phone accuracy.
entries.condition: 66% is speaker A's word-based visual-decoding accuracy; the intelligibility trial itself uses correct phonetic transcription, not this predicted sequence.
entries.quote: With a visual phone recognizer accuracy of 66% though (corresponding to speaker A in the word-based decoding scenario), consistently intelligible synthesis is as yet not possible.

entries.text: The authors concede that a proper final intelligibility validation needs more listeners, more test material, and unpredictable sentences.
entries.condition: Current evaluation has seven listeners and 20 test sentences selected randomly from the test database.

entries.text: The authors say the sub-one-hour dictionary lacks sufficient phonetic-context variety for completely natural-sounding output and that the system is not yet fully functional.
entries.value: less than 1 hour of speech data
entries.condition: Refers to corpus-based unit selection examples and the limited audiovisual training dictionary.

entries.text: The authors suggest performance could improve on a limited-vocabulary task of fewer than 250 words, but describe this as future testing rather than a measured result.
entries.condition: Prospective application; no such experiment is reported in this paper.

entries.text: All experiments use uttered speech; the authors state that evaluation on genuinely silent speech, whispered or unvocalized, remains necessary.
entries.condition: No silent-speech, whispered-speech, or laryngectomized-participant evaluation is reported.

entries.text: A future Ultraspeech acquisition system is described as supporting more than 60 fps and interactive inter-session recalibration to enable larger multi-session databases; it is not the system evaluated here.
entries.unit: frames per second for both ultrasound and optical streams
entries.condition: Prospective system under test/development; current experiments use the analog 29.97 Hz setup.

entries.text: The authors present an ultrasound-based SSI driven by tongue and lip observations as a feasible approach, while explicitly limiting that conclusion to current experiments and oracle/strong recognition conditions.
entries.condition: Paper concludes current recognition is not sufficiently accurate for systematic intelligibility, and silent speech remains unevaluated.
entries.quote: a segmental vocoder driven by visual observations of the tongue and lips is a reasonable approach for making an SSI.

entries.text: No random seed is reported for the random selection of the 20 synthesis test sentences; no stochastic training seed or repeated-run seed is given.
entries.condition: Jackknife phone-recognition evaluation and random selection of synthesis test sentences; exact randomization implementation is not stated.

entries.text: There is no held-out-speaker evaluation: lists are split within each speaker database, so each recognition fold trains and tests on sentences from the same speaker.
entries.condition: The paper presents separate database A and B results, not cross-speaker transfer or speaker-independent recognition.

entries.text: The paper describes grayscale conversion, resizing, PCA coding, and derivatives but does not specify per-feature centering, scaling, or normalization before HMM training and evaluation.
entries.condition: Applies to the visual feature sequence; explicit normalization details for acoustic MFCCs are also absent.

entries.text: No chance-level recognition or intelligibility baseline is reported.
entries.condition: Phone recognition and word-based listener transcription results; the acoustic decoder is a comparator, not a chance baseline.

entries.text: Although PCA frames are said to be selected as a phonetically balanced subset, the paper does not say whether PCA bases are fitted separately inside each recognition training fold or on all available frames.
entries.condition: Potential train/test dependence for image coding; the paper gives no fold-specific PCA construction protocol.
entries.quote: In order to guarantee a better exploration of the possible vocal tract configurations, this subset is constructed so as to be phonetically balanced.

entries.text: The two validation fold indices and the aggregation rule for the reported jackknife performance are not specified; the paper does not clarify pooled counts versus an average across test folds.
entries.condition: Two of 26 jackknife experiments selected for tuning Gaussian counts and transition penalties.

entries.text: No user confirmation or acceptance stage is described or evaluated between decoded output and speech generation.
entries.condition: The described pipeline goes from phone decoding to unit selection and waveform generation.

entries.text: No user-facing correction or repair mechanism for recognition or synthesis errors is described or evaluated.
entries.condition: The system output is generated directly from the predicted phone sequence and selected units.

entries.text: The authors identify stabilizing the ultrasound transducer and camera relative to the vocal tract as a major challenge for a wearable system.
entries.condition: The experiment used a fixed HATS setup and a single long session; a portable apparatus is future work.

entries.text: Palatal reference traces were collected by 10 cc water swallows during short breaks every 90 sentences; four separated traces per speaker were manually extracted and overlaid to monitor probe/head drift.
entries.unit: water volume; sentence interval; traces per speaker
entries.condition: Manual palatal-trace monitoring during a single long session; it is not an inter-session recalibration mechanism.

entries.text: Phone [ng] averages 126 ms and is represented by three or four source images, giving each of the three emitting HMM states a distinct trajectory segment.
entries.condition: 30 fps acquisition with interpolated 100 Hz visual features; compared with the shorter [t] phone.

entries.text: The conclusion summarizes that with about 60% of phones correctly identified, the system cannot systematically produce an intelligible synthesis.
entries.condition: Authors' general conclusion for continuous uttered speech; distinct from the 66% speaker-A word-based result and oracle-phone synthesis test.
entries.quote: with some 60% of phones correctly identified in a sequence of tongue and lip images, the system is not able to systematically provide an intelligible synthesis.

entries.text: Target and concatenation costs are manually weighted, but the paper gives no tuning procedure or validation/selection data for choosing their relative weights.
entries.condition: The described evaluation tests synthesis with oracle phones; no weight sensitivity or held-out weight-selection experiment is reported.

entries.text: The rare phoneme [zh] occurred 52 times in the database and was grouped with [sh] for scoring equivalence-class confusions.
entries.condition: Phone recognition scoring; [sh]/[zh] within-class confusions were not counted as errors.

entries.text: The authors claim ultrasound is well suited to vocal-tract imaging because it is non-invasive, clinically safe, and has good time resolution.
entries.condition: Motivating rationale; these properties are not separately measured in the reported SSI evaluation.

entries.text: The authors focus their interpretation on database A because B was affected by acquisition difficulties.
entries.condition: Speaker B transducer shift; results for both reported
entries.quote: The interpretations and discussions in the remainder of the article will focus on database A, which was recorded without any of these experimental difficulties.

entries.text: The synthesis test isolates unit selection and HNM generation by using correct phonetic labels for 20 test sentences.
entries.condition: oracle phone labels; speaker not stated
entries.quote: In order to independently evaluate only the proposed synthesis framework, i.e. the unit selection algorithm and the HNM-based waveform generation with prosodic adaptation, 20 test sentences  are re-synthesized from their visual data alone, after first labeling it with the correct phonetic transcription.

entries.text: The target cites its own 2009 multi-stream work as current study, not as a compared system.
The segmental route is motivated by the state of the art of text-to-speech synthesis; no direct articulatory-to-acoustic mapping is discussed or compared.
entries.condition: Introduction; no direct-mapping baseline in Secs. 5-6

entries.text: HMM-based synthesis is mentioned as a preliminary alternative that avoids the hard decision; no comparison is reported.
entries.quote: In a recent, preliminary study, we have also experimented with HMM-based synthesis (Tokuda et al., 2000), which avoids this “hard decision” problem, and appears thus far to also be promising in our application.

entries.text: Original sentences were transcribed at 97% average accuracy; synthesized results are given only in Fig. 10.
entries.condition: seven listeners, 20 original sentences
entries.quote: The average recognition accuracy of the original sentences was 97%, which gives an idea of the upper bound for this intelligibility test.

entries.text: EMA articulator positions are mapped to the vocal-tract spectrum by searching an articulatory-acoustic database and interpolating the selected samples.
entries.condition: one male Japanese speaker; 9 coils; LSP from 12-order LPC
entries.quote: the database samples that are coincidental with the input articulator

entries.text: Synthesis with phoneme categorization restricting the database search was preferred in 84% of pairs by ten listeners over ten sentences.
entries.condition: ten subjects, ten sentences, pairwise with vs without categorization
entries.quote: The result was that 84% of sp eech stim uli synthesized with phoneme categorization were preferred in quality to those without categorization

entries.text: Spectral error between estimated and actual spectra: mean 2.24 dB, SD 1.31 dB (30-order cepstrum distance).
entries.condition: leave-one-utterance-out over the data set, one speaker

entries.text: One male Japanese speaker, 488 utterances.
entries.condition: single speaker

entries.text: Articulatory parameters and pitch are mapped to LSPs by linear estimation or neural networks.
entries.condition: one female Swedish speaker; EMA plus motion capture
entries.quote: Two training methods were tested, linear estimation (section 4.1) and neural networks (section 4.2).

entries.text: Evaluation by LSP correlation and informal subjective judgment.
entries.condition: no formal listener test
entries.quote: The synthesis was evaluated statistically by the correlation between the original and estimated line spectrum pairs and perceptually, by informal subjective judgment.

entries.text: Context-dependent multi-stream HMMs identify 65.6% of phones (open vocabulary) and 74.7% with a 2.5k-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: one speaker, 61 minutes, first 1020 CMU-Arctic sentences; concurrent (2009-09)
entries.quote: the system is able to correctly identify 65,6% of the phones from visual information only

entries.text: Table 1 P row: CI feature fusion 57.7/67.4, CD feature fusion 62.6/70.6, CI-MSHMM 59.5/71.1, CD-MSHMM 65.6/74.7 (unconstrained/constrained).
entries.condition: one speaker; unconstrained and 2.5k-word constrained decoding

entries.text: Database: one speaker, first 1020 CMU-Arctic sentences, 61 minutes after cleanup.
entries.quote: After cleanup of the recordings, the database contains 61 minutes of speech contained in 109553 bitmap frames.

entries.text: Combined context-dependent and multi-stream modelling gives 8 points absolute over the CI feature-fusion baseline.
entries.quote: Compared to a baseline system based on context-independent models and a feature fusion strategy, this new approach has led to a 8% absolute performance improvement.

entries.text: Continuous EMG recognition with context-independent phone HMMs bootstrapped from audio alignments and a trigram LM.
entries.condition: one speaker, one session
entries.quote: Since the training set is very small, we only trained context-independent acoustic models.

entries.text: Decoding with a trigram Broadcast News LM.
entries.quote: The trained acoustic model was used together with a trigram BN language model for decoding.

entries.text: EMG phone models are 3-state left-to-right HMMs.
entries.condition: concurrent (2009-12)

entries.text: 6.17% WER on the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge benchmark with denoising convolutional autoencoder features.
entries.condition: SSC benchmark test set, Kaldi DNN-HMM, WSJ 5k bigram LM; later (2019)

entries.quote: However, even if some sentences were well transcribed (especially the short ones and those containing “common words”), this preliminary subjective evaluation revealed that it was not possible to synthesize intelligible speech “consistently”, neither with the GMM-based mapping approach, nor with the HMM-based approach.

entries.text: Three listeners transcribed 15 synthesized test sentences.
Neural decoder outputs F1/F2 that drive a Klatt formant synthesizer (direct mapping).

questions.q: Which database was used for the synthesis test, and is an aggregate synthesized-speech accuracy given in the text?
questions.answer: Speaker not stated in Sec. 5.3; interpretation focuses on database A (Sec. 4.2). No aggregate synthesized accuracy in the text; only Fig. 10.

questions.q: Why were context-dependent models not trained?
questions.answer: Small training sets (< 1 hour), even with tying.

questions.q: Does the target mention its own 2009 multi-stream / context-dependent work?
questions.answer: Yes, as current study of fusion; no comparison.

questions.q: Is a direct articulatory-to-acoustic mapping discussed as an alternative?
questions.answer: No; segmental route motivated by TTS state of the art; HMM-based synthesis mentioned as preliminary.

questions.q: Kaburagi 1998 and Engwall 2005: input, mapping, evaluation, speakers?
questions.answer: Both map measured articulation directly to LSPs, one speaker each; Kaburagi restricts a database search by phoneme categorization (84% preference), Engwall uses linear/ANN with informal judgment.
CI feature fusion 57.7/67.4, CD 62.6/70.6, CI-MSHMM 59.5/71.1, CD-MSHMM 65.6/74.7, one speaker, 61 minutes.
